en: The Biography of the Layman Zhou Anshi (Zhou Mengyan).

His given name was Sirén, his courtesy name Anshi, and he was a student of the classics from Kunshan. He was extensively versed in the sutras and the Tripitaka and possessed deep faith in the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
He styled himself the Layman Huaixi. He once [reflected that] while sentient beings commit immeasurable transgressions, only...

The two karmas of lust and killing truly occupy the greater portion [of human conduct]. Consequently, he composed two treatises on the precepts against killing and lust; the treatise on the prohibition of killing is titled *Wànshàn Xiānzī* (The Prerequisite for All Goodness).
Its words are mostly earnest, sincere, and deeply poignant. He stated that whenever he passed by any shrine, he would invariably offer this prayer:
"I only pray that the honored deity will give rise to a supramundane mind and refrain from receiving offerings of blood; may you single-mindedly and constantly recite the name of Amitābha."

To Amitābha Buddha. Seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, I, Sirin, from this year at twenty-four until the end of my life, vow that if in the interim I should kill even a single small fish or shrimp, or even if among my family members at home a single person should harm a single mosquito or ant—may the Honored Deity investigate and punish me, and may a swift thunderbolt shatter the wooden boards upon which I write. Sirin himself...
I am now twenty-four years old. Until the end of my life, when I see fish by the river or birds looking up toward the sky, may I never fail to contemplate their deliverance;

instead, may I not give rise to the intent to kill. I likewise take this vow: from this year of my twenty-fourth year until the end of my life, even within my dreams, if I see someone killing a living being, may I be unable to refrain from sincerely reciting the name of the Buddha and resolving to deliver them.
Yet they instead rejoice and support such matters, making a vow identical to this. As for the treatise on the prohibition of lust, it is titled *The Return from Madness in the Sea of Desire*.
It exhorts those who are lustful to first contemplate the prison of the womb and fully understand its manifold sufferings; this is called the preliminary expedient for ceasing lust.
Next, one contemplates this body, where various worms swarm and gather, writhing and moving about, devouring the brain and marrow of humans; this is [the contemplation of impurity].
First, one begins with the preparatory method of contemplating impurity. Next, one contemplates how the bodies of men and women are filled with pus, blood, mucus, and saliva;
they are like latrines and cesspools, abodes of filth and excrement. This is the preparatory method for counteracting lust.

Next, one visualizes a dead person lying flat on their back, the cold penetrating to the very bones, yellow fluid flowing out, the stench unbearable to smell, and worms growing all over the body in every place.

They bore into and gnawed at it until the skin and flesh were gradually consumed, leaving the bones and joints scattered in all directions; eventually, the tomb was breached and the bones emerged, to be trampled by humans and beasts.

My own body, too, will ultimately be like this. Next, I reflected upon the causes and conditions explained in the Lotus Sutra regarding the characteristics of arising and the characteristics of cessation.
This non-arising and non-ceasing is the expedient means for severing lust and exhausting its source.
Next, one contemplates oneself within a lotus flower inside a pond of the seven treasures in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

As the lotus flower blossoms, one sees Amitābha Buddha seated upon a precious lotus, together with various kinds of adorned auspicious signs. One also sees oneself prostrating and making offerings to the Buddha.
While performing this contemplation, he made a vow to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss to forever escape the pit of lust;
this is the expedient means for ultimate liberation. Furthermore, he had previously compiled the *Direct Guide to the Western Return* in four fascicles.

In the first month of the fourth year of the Qianlong era, he took leave of his family, saying he was about to depart for the West. When his family requested that he bathe with scented water, he declined, saying, "I am [already] fragrant..."
Tang bathed for a long time; he passed away while chatting and laughing. A rare fragrance wafted intensely, filling the entire room.
He was eighty-four years old. Image Eulogy (Yushan): Zhang Erdan (Meyu).
The various works composed by Master Anshi of Kunshan have truly provided me with no small measure of benefit as I read and received them.
In the past, the World-Honored One even sacrificed his body as an offering for the sake of a half-gāthā;
yet, regarding the kindness of this Master, I am utterly at a loss to know how I might repay it. Thus says Wang Zishi Xin.

Upon being requested to provide a colophon for this portrait, I was filled with joy and wonder as I gazed upon it in worship. I have respectfully composed these twenty verses in the four-character style;

they do not begin to express even a ten-thousandth part of Master [Zhou] Dunyi’s greatness. My intent is merely to propagate the spirit of his writings and to once again establish the karmic conditions for rebirth in the Pure Land.
I imagine that from within the Hall of Purple Gold, you would surely smile at me from afar. Written by [Dao].

On the second day after the first day of the last month of winter in the year of Gengzi, this Great Layman was born during the Kangxi era. His talent and eloquence were unimpeded; he was able to bestow the Dharma through both pen and tongue.

Like a thunderclap and a flash of lightning, he had thoroughly recited and mastered the scriptures of the Three Teachings. His spirit surged like gathering clouds, and his eloquence flowed like surging waves.

Acting as an envoy of the Tathāgata, he served as a great guide. Alas! In this age of the Dharma’s decline, sentient beings are ignorant and deluded; were it not for Bodhisattvas such as these, [the world would be lost].

Who roars like a lion? He has returned to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). How could my own birth be considered late? His writings amount to ten thousand words; they are the resources for awakening.
Having heard his discourses in the past, I now behold his graceful form. With staff and bamboo hat, he travels westward, his snowy beard fluttering in the wind. Among my disciples, I am...
The virtuous one is praised in private; with heads bowed and tears falling, her name is identical to that of Buddhadhara. All we who share this same aspiration revere and look up to her.

Although this is but a painted image, the conditions for its existence lie herein. That she possesses the power of aspiration is difficult to conceive or fathom. What is manifested here is merely the form depicted.
Lotus branches surge upward; who could not prostrate before them? He gathers all in with compassion, and hundreds of millions of beings hasten toward the precious pond in the West.
(Gugu) Zhu Zhaogeng (Yinbai): Having cast off his shoes, he returned to An-yang;
his lofty style is spoken of to this day. His writings are equal to the Buddha’s verses; his love for all things expresses his compassionate heart.

The body has already transcended the mundane world; the spirit returns to a profound salvation of the age. As one touches the remaining images, there remain the lingering echoes of his coughs and spittle.
(Yuanhe period) Qiu Hongye (style name: Youchi):

The moon of nature is wondrously luminous, fully possessed by every person. Through sincere devotion and accumulated cultivation, he attained the awakening of the sages. Untainted by even a single speck of dust.
Transcending the mundane while remaining within it—this is the aspiration of the layman, the venerable elder of Lukcheng. Moved by great compassion, he has cultivated immeasurable merit.

Having preceded those who tread the path of Longshu, he now leads those who follow the "measuring wood. His towering golden terrace alone marks his lofty footsteps. May all beings throughout the great trichiliocosm universally aspire to this.
Freed from defilement and impurity, when the fruits of goodness are perfected, one is reborn together in Sukhāvatī.
(Yuanhe) Zhu Zhaobiao (Weiqing): The river of craving flows ever deeper;
the waves of suffering splash ever higher. Alas for Jambudvīpa! The habits of the five corruptions are difficult to transform.
Master Wei rose from Lucheng, alone vowing the Bodhisattva’s aspiration. He personally composed four types of writings, in every word embodying both warning and exhortation.
They are like a brilliant torch or a flash of lightning within a dark chamber; they are like a hand reaching down with a white silk cord to aid one falling from a precipice.
Having saved himself, he saves others; his compassionate heart manifests through pity. Once the fruits of goodness are realized, the lotus pedestal is refined gold.
Later generations lose their standard; they can only privately admire him with empty longing. How virtuous was the Elder of Stone Heart! His descendants searched for him everywhere.
In joyful surprise, I have obtained the true likeness. Entrusted to the skillful hand of a master calligrapher, my own life has been born too late; I have had no way to behold his sacred countenance.
Thus, I manifest my sincere heart; opening this book is like seeing him face to face. Moreover, now that I behold this portrait, I prostrate myself in worship, giving rise to deep devotion.

I prostrate twice and silently offer these words: May you grant the convenience of this bridge and raft to lead the multitudes of Sahā to ascend together to the stage of non-retrogression. (Lishui) Qiu Sunjin (Zhutang).
Having read the Master’s letter three times, I prostrate again before the Master’s portrait. Your benevolent words bring benefit far and wide; your countenance of the Way is serene and radiant.

He has extensively cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva. At times he manifests in the guise of a layman, moving between the Confucian and Buddhist worlds, yet ultimately he shall return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
Alas for Jambudvīpa, where beings drift through the suffering of birth and death; his bequeathed writings fill the world, resonating like the sound of a celestial drum.

My birth has already brought regret; it is too late. I have not yet been able to attend upon you with staff and mat. For twenty years on the path of the Deer City, I have merely yearned with deep sincerity to look up to you as one gazes at a high mountain.

With reverence, I burn this single incense offering and pray with uplifted devotion to the Flower Treasury (Avataṃsaka). May you return to enter the Sahā world and deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
The lay practitioner Fang Buying (Xiaoxiang) of Kunshan was a gentleman of our own locality.
With his lofty character before my eyes, I held him in the highest esteem. The literary style of our region is as exquisite as the Jade Peak;
in recent times, eminent figures have arisen one after another. Zhuangqu attained the true transmission of Neo-Confucian learning, and Bolu followed in his footsteps. Each...

In terms of specific prose writing, Guo Zhunchuan stands alone. Guo Tinglin’s scholarship was exhaustive in its examination of the classics and histories; the Layman (Zhang Dai) further mastered both Confucianism and Buddhism.
Having perceived the nature of life and destiny and attained liberation from birth and death, he authored two works on the precepts against killing and lust.

With a single, thunderous shout, he struck directly at the core, delivering these sentient beings across the ford of delusion. Later, he pointed directly to the path of the Western Paradise: "One mind."
Reciting the Buddha’s name while heading toward the Land of Bliss, ten million *buddhakṣetras* are as close as the span of a palm. Within the ponds of the seven treasures, lotus flowers bloom;
laughing and speaking with his family, he says, "The Buddha is coming! Sixty years after my birth, I regret not having personally met the Tathāgata’s messenger.
Ultimately, my private devotion to him is nothing other than this: the causal conditions for transcending the world lie herein.
The Layman styles himself "Huaisi" (Embracing the West); my own longing lies with the Layman.

(Zhou Xianghai of Wu County), whose heart is like incense, has manifested in the body of a layperson (*upāsaka*) as a donor of the Dharma. Since the time of Longshu, there has been none but our Master who exhorts others toward the Pure Land.

To transform those of initial capacity, he used the hook of desire to lead them into the Buddha’s wisdom. The Master first pointed directly to the nature of mind, so that those of the three capacities might all be equally benefited;
he then employed causes, conditions, and parables to cause them to abide therein. Mr. Wang, with a profound heart, embroidered this image for worship, intending to inform all people of the world.
Each should respect and have faith in the Chan Master Guan (Jue'a), a spiritual friend outside the mundane world and a Great Bodhisattva,
who wears the scholar’s cap while preaching the Buddha-dharma and upholds the *prātimokṣa* by forbidding sexual misconduct and killing— this is the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

The teaching is profound and comprehensive in its intent. He dedicated his body and mind to serve every speck of dust and every corner of the universe; he propagated the practice of reciting the Name and elevated the Lotus School.

Like the spear of Lu Yang, the sun was made to turn back toward noon. Reading the Master’s writings is as if seeing him in person; bowing before his portrait, the spirit of the Way fills one. Before him was Longshu; after him comes Chimu.

While you stood in the center of the state, the Three Jewels were like the three legs of a tripod. When the teaching of the Buddha declined, you and your peers arose to do so. You silenced heterodox doctrines and revitalized sagging customs. A hundred years have passed since I followed in your footsteps;

beholding your remaining portrait and caressing your surviving writings, my heart is filled with both sorrow and joy, and my tears flow in streams. Your aspirations were directed toward the West, and mine are likewise.
I pray that you will extend your protection and cause my lotus to blossom.
(Dongmao) Zhu Dayun: A single mat of tea smoke rises from my silvering hair. For years I have laughed at the folly of the fly returning to its old tracks.
Now that all the burdens of Zhou and He are settled, I shall forever pay homage to the Teacher within the cold forest.
(Fengzhou) Feng Xusheng: Formerly, I read your collected works;
at that time, I cherished the friendship of a superior man. Your benevolent words moistened all things, and your profound arguments awakened the blind masses.

Beholding this likeness today, my heart feels as if it had been drawn toward it in a former life. In years to come, when the land is a pure and prosperous kingdom, I shall look up with longing to welcome you.
(Renhe) Hu Ting (Tingchen): A single sheet transmits the image;
joyfully I behold my Master. Following in his dust, I cherish my admiration; my sincere vow is to journey westward.

The books left behind to propagate the teachings remain; the memorials submitted to benefit the people endure. Burning incense, I gaze upon the model of the Way; his vigorous spirit appears with its white eyebrows.

Long have I cherished the image of the embroidered silks; now I behold the true countenance in detail. He transmits the precious raft across the waters of delusion; in this final age, he turns back the surging flood.

To imitate his gait and movements is relatively easy; to move the hearts of the stubborn and the incorruptible is uniquely difficult. After ten years, my long-cherished wish has been fulfilled; I have finally entrusted this work to the carver for publication.

(Ten years ago, I met the late gentleman’s great-grandson, the young scholar Shao Rong. From him, I obtained these posthumous drafts. Furthermore, at the residence of Mr. Wang Shixin, I made a tracing of the deceased’s portrait. Not long after, Shao Rong passed away. I intended to have these drafts set in print.)

After a long time, this had not been accomplished. Now, with the assistance of Wang Xinchi and Shen Jizhi, who provided the funds for the carving of the printing blocks, the collation and printing of these collected writings have been completed.
I respectfully compose two verses in the *gu* (ancient) style: Wang Fengzhang (Xinchi) of Gusu has finally fulfilled his long-cherished wish to see the West.
The blossoms of the Dharma open a springtime that endures through ten thousand kalpas. With compassion he extends salvation to all people and things; His universal benefit reaches both gods and men.

In this illusion and dream, who can be pitied? To those lost on the path, I grant leave to ask for the ford. Like you, O Master, whose compassion spans mountains and seas, all deliberations are but a mere speck of dust.

Yet since his remaining writings still exist, I venture to publish them for my own edification. His eloquence was so powerful it knew no obstruction; that his hidden virtue now shines forth was never delayed.
The brush and ink flow from the mind; smoke and clouds follow the wrist. Reading this single volume three times over, one finds that the seeds of the lotus surely contain nourishment.
Wang Dashen’s grief and intensity are extreme; it is as if he had received it from the golden mouth of our Buddha, the World-Honored One, and attained the six kinds [of supernormal powers] thereby.

along the banks of the ponds, flowering trees and nets of trees proclaim the sound of virtue,
while fragrant waters, flowers, and birds chant verses of praise.
The scene is sublime; one naturally partakes of food and drink as appropriate,
practices the cultivation of contemplation on voice, countenance, and physical form,
and by seeing the Buddha through visualization and reciting His name, one beholds the Buddha.

a person of great filial piety does not wish to enter a womb; a person of great nobility must know how to feel self-reproach."

The World-Honored One appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause: out of compassion for sentient beings wandering in the cycle of the six realms.

The first doubt:

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their primary activity. If they wish to deliver sentient beings, they should simply vow to be born within the triple world, amidst the five turbidities and the three miserable realms, to rescue suffering beings. For what reason, then, do they seek birth in the Pure Land?
If one acts solely for one’s own benefit and abandons sentient beings, would this not constitute a deficiency in great compassion and an obstruction to the path to enlightenment?

Answer: There are two kinds of bodhisattvas. The first are those who have long practiced as bodhisattvas, who have already drawn near to various Buddhas and attained the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

The second are those bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds [on enlightenment], who have never yet drawn near to various Buddhas and have not yet attained [the realization of the non-arising of dharmas].
Those who possess the patience of the dharma of birth are bodhisattvas who have practiced for a long time;

possessing great supernormal powers and great majestic authority, they are able to manifest as devas, rishis, emperors, kings, ghosts, or animals. Thus, they enter and exit the cycle of birth and death to extensively deliver sentient beings.
As for those who are beginners in practice, their strength is shallow and slight; although they have resolved upon the mind of a bodhisattva, they still abide in the stage of ordinary worldlings.
If one cannot save oneself from one's own illness, how can one save others? Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"It is impossible for an ordinary person bound by all fetters to possess a heart of great compassion and vow to be born in a turbid age to rescue suffering sentient beings. Why is this?
Within the five turbidities, sounds, forms, wealth, and profit entangle one at every moment; the enemies of affliction are densely arrayed in layers. Briefly...
A single misstep leads directly to downfall. Even if one is reborn among humans, it is difficult to encounter an age in which a Buddha has appeared.
Even if a Buddha does appear in the world, it is difficult to give rise to a mind of faith and inclination.

Should one fortunately develop faith in the Buddha-vehicle and practice the life of renunciation, yet subsequently be reborn into a state of great wealth and high status, one cannot avoid becoming attached to worldly conditions and extensively committing various evils. From [this point...]
Once this human body is lost, when will one ever again attain liberation? Therefore, those with wisdom who wish to deliver sentient beings first seek to see the Buddha.

If they can indeed achieve single-mindedness without distraction and attain rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha, their karma will already have been transformed into an indestructible diamond body;
only then may they fulfill their vow to deliver beings according to their various types. It is like rescuing someone drowning: one must first [ensure one's own safety].
Only by boarding a boat or raft can one lead others out of the water; if one merely attempts to rescue people from a well, there are none who do not drown along with them.
This is not a lack of compassion; it is precisely the skillful application of compassion.
The second inquiry: All phenomena are empty in essence; they are originally unarisen, equal, and quiescent. Why, then, do you abandon this to seek that, desiring to be born in the Western Land?
A sutra says: "When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. If you wish to seek a pure land, you should first purify [your own mind].

Is it not that you alone reject the former while seeking the latter? If one says there is nothing to be sought in either this or that, this is to cling to the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
If one says there is nothing to be abandoned in either this or that, this is to cling to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Though one knows that the lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates the pure land and teaches and transforms all classes of living beings. Therefore, although...

If we speak of phenomena, rather than purifying this mind to dwell within the five [realms],...
In this age of defilement and evil, how can one purify this mind to dwell in the Lotus Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Moreover, for those dwelling in a turbid world who seek purity yet fail to attain it, how much more so for those in the Lotus Land who do not seek purity and are naturally pure?
The third doubt:
Since the merits of all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions are equal, why not universally recollect all merits to be born in all pure lands,
rather than seeking the pure land of a single Buddha exclusively?

Answer: The pure lands of all Buddhas are indeed all equal. However, because the faculties of sentient beings are dull and those who are turbid and distracted are many, if one does not concentrate the mind on a single point, samādhi will be difficult to achieve.
Therefore, single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha Buddha is itself the "Samādhi of One Aspect. The *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One's Vows* states:
"The Bodhisattva Puguang asked the Buddha: 'In the ten directions there are pure lands everywhere; why is it that... [text continues].
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you exclusively praise the Pure Land of Amitābha in the west and specifically exhort beings to be reborn there? The Buddha told Puguang:

“The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa have minds that are largely turbid and distracted. For this reason, I exclusively praise the Pure Land of a single Buddha in the west, so that these sentient beings may concentrate their minds on a single object and easily attain rebirth. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: “The bodies of all Buddhas are...”
This is the body of a single Buddha, which is like the pure, full moon universally reflected in all waters.
Therefore, know that to mind one Buddha is to mind all Buddhas; to be born in one pure land is no different from being born in all pure lands.
The fourth inquiry:

Thus, people of the present Sahā world who recite the Buddha’s name with faith will inevitably invoke the name of Amitābha. As for sentient beings of the future whose merit will be meager, the Dharma...
When the Dharma is about to perish, all the various sutras shall depart; only the *Amitābha Sūtra* shall remain for another hundred years. What is the proof of this?

First, it is because of the instruction of our original teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Among the vast teachings of the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the canon, there is but this single method of holding the name:
not recollecting other Buddhas, but recollecting only Amitābha. If this were not the case...
This is of the utmost importance. Why do you speak so repeatedly and earnestly? First, it is because the Buddhas of the ten directions all act as witnesses.

Thus, if one wishes to cultivate the Pure Land...

ordinary beings bound by all fetters possess heavy and thick evil karma; they have not severed any of their afflictions, nor do they possess even a hair’s breadth of merit.

It has not yet been cultivated. Answer: This relies upon the power of Amitābha Buddha; it does not depend on one's own power.

It is like a lame person walking along a road who cannot travel even several li all day long, yet if they ride the Elephant-Treasure of a Cakravartin King, they can traverse the four great continents in a single morning.

If one practices the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, it requires only diligent cultivation with a single-minded focus free from distraction; one can then attain rebirth in the present life, proceeding directly from the West to practice forevermore.
To fall back and regress until one finally attains Buddhahood is the most circuitous route. It is like a worm inside a bamboo stalk that wishes to exit upward;
it must gnaw through countless nodes, enduring unbearable suffering. If it were to recognize a way from the side, it could gnaw through and emerge horizontally with great ease.
Therefore, those who practice the Pure Land method are said to "emerge horizontally" from the triple world. Why is this so?
One might doubt that ordinary beings are unable to achieve rebirth [in the Pure Land].
This is the sixth inquiry.
Among the nine grades, those of the lower three grades are mostly evil persons who, solely by virtue of reciting the Buddha's name at the time of death, [attain rebirth].
Regarding rebirth there: what if, once born in that land, one still possesses wrong views and the three poisons?

Third, because the jewel trees, flowers, and birds all proclaim the sublime Dharma. Fourth, because they have only Bodhisattvas as virtuous friends and evil conditions are forever severed.
Fifth, because their lifespan is long and far-reaching, allowing them to practice and cultivate through successive kalpas.
Thus, there is a profound reason why those who are born in the Western Land will proceed directly to Buddhahood, never regressing. This is indeed for a good cause.

If ordinary beings have extensively created immeasurable evil karma in past lives and in this present life, how can they achieve [liberation] through ten recitations at the moment of death?
Thus, they attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

On the contrary, they encounter a virtuous friend who teaches them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Even if they are thus taught to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, how could they possibly listen with faith?

They will cast aside all worldly entangments at once, recognizing only the single path to the Western Paradise as the place to which they can turn back, with no other destination possible.

The Land of Ultimate Bliss is separated from this Sahā world by as many as ten trillion Buddha-fields.
Given such vast distance, how can ordinary beings reach it? Furthermore, we have heard that women, those with physical deficiencies, and those of the two vehicles [cannot be reborn there].
None of them will attain rebirth there. Is this not true? Answer:

That which is distant and difficult to traverse is the physical body; that which can reach in a single thought-moment is the mind. Those who practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) are born in that land solely by means of this mind;
it is not by carrying this physical frame along with them. It is like a person dreaming of traveling to another country.
Even if one is thousands of miles away, a single call will cause them to awaken. How could it be that awakening is easy when the Way is near, yet difficult when the Way is far?
Regarding the statement that "women and those with physical deficiencies are not born [there]," this means that in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are no women or those with physical deficiencies;

The flavor of the Dharma. One must sever [afflictions] so that they do not, on the contrary, sow the roots of calamity.

Those who speak of wearying of and leaving the turbid world—within this turbid and evil age, thorns arise at every turn. Worldly people spend their entire lives in hardship for the sake of the two matters of food and clothing;

they spend their whole existence rushing about for the sake of fame and profit. With hands flailing and feet stumbling, they willingly become domestic slaves to their wives and children, brooding over them day and night.

Dream-like thoughts collectively constitute the afflictions that seek out the physical body. One imagines one's own form to be seven feet tall, yet its exterior is merely wrapped in a single sheet of skin;

thus, one falsely regards oneself as great and noble. If one were to observe with the divine eye, one would see that within, there is nothing more than a belly full of urine, excrement, pus, blood, and foul secretions. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Such is the city of the body."
The rākṣasas of ignorance dwell therein; how could one possessed of wisdom take pleasure in this body, rather than regarding it with revulsion and seeking liberation?
As for those who aspire to and delight in the Land of Bliss, the joy of the West is not comparable to that of the celestial palaces;
it cannot be described by words. Each day, simply take what is spoken in the sutras and contemplate each point in stillness.
Thinking, "I shall certainly come here in the future," the thought of longing and admiration will naturally arise, and the karmic conditions for the Pure Land will naturally ripen.
What is meant by "generating the bodhicitta"? The *Treatise on Rebirth* states: "Bodhicitta is the mind that vows to attain Buddhahood.
To vow to attain Buddhahood means to feel compassion for all sentient beings who wander through the six realms of rebirth and undergo suffering.

Suffering is boundless; therefore, one resolves to rescue and deliver others, enabling them to transcend the three realms and together reach the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West, and only then does one rest.

If those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha can possess these two kinds of mindfulness power and further give rise to the bodhicitta, emulating the Tathāgata’s intent to deliver sentient beings, how could they fail to attain rebirth with certainty?
"It has never happened that anyone was granted a prediction of Buddhahood by the Buddha [without practicing Pure Land]. The above concludes the *Ten Doubts Treatise*.
A guest asked the Elder Tianru: "Master Yongming Youshou was universally esteemed within the realm as a patriarchal master.
Yet he personally cultivated the Pure Land and taught others to do so, saying: 'If one has Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten will go astray on the path.'"

If it is said that there is no need for meditation and yet there is the Pure Land, such that ten thousand who practice will all be delivered, does this not mean that one is demeaning one's own meditation while over-praising the Pure Land?
Answer: The Great Master Yongming did not over-praise it. The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is most extensive and vast. Regarding the cultivation of the Pure Land...
The Dharma is most simple and easy. As for its vastness, it encompasses all capacities and conditions without exception:

from Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment above, down to the ignorant and the common folk, even those who have committed the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds—should they recite the Buddha’s name and repent at the moment of death, there are none who do not attain rebirth.
As for its simplicity, it is initially free from difficult or arduous practices; one need only maintain...
By merely reciting these six characters of the Name, one shall immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land, achieve the stage of non-retrogression, and continue until the attainment of Buddhahood.
I ask you: could there be any practice for transcending the world more expedient than this? Were it not for Chan Master Shou, he would not have been able to cultivate himself by means of this;
were it not for Chan Master Shou, he would not have been able to teach others by means of this.

Question: I have already heard your instructions regarding the vastness and simplicity [of the Pure Land method]. However, as for those of the Chan school who have attained awakening and realized the nature, since it is said that "seeing one's nature is itself becoming a Buddha," why must they further seek the Pure Land?
Answer: It is precisely because one has attained awakening that one aspires for rebirth there. You have simply not yet awakened.
Were you to awaken, the momentum toward the Pure Land would be such that ten thousand oxen could not turn it back.

Furthermore, do you believe that after a single awakening, all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are eliminated, all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, and the enmities accumulated over immeasurable kalpas are dissolved, so that you will never again undergo future existence (*punarbhava*)? Or...
Or is it that because there are still remaining karmic bonds and unfinished deeds, one cannot avoid receiving heavy retribution for light offenses?

Furthermore, does one immediately possess the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics upon a single awakening, thereby subduing the heavenly Māras and delivering the worlds of the ten directions?
Or is it that the power of one's supernatural penetrations is not yet fully realized at once, and one must still await future lives and subsequent ages?

Furthermore, if one were to claim that the Great Matter is already completed with a single awakening, then the great bodhisattvas who have extensively cultivated the six perfections for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust would, by contrast, appear inferior to you.

The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi-sūtra* records the account of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s own past causes, wherein he states that he attained the Buddha-recollection samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). The World-Honored One then bestowed upon him this prediction: "You shall go..."

One is born in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* records that the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, through the Ten Great Vows (*daśa-mahāpraṇidhāna*), instructed the youth Sudhana, concluding likewise by guiding him back to Ultimate Bliss.

Within the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the World-Honored One bestowed a prophecy upon Nāgārjuna, also including words regarding rebirth in Ultimate Bliss. As for the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, the World-Honored One granted his seal of approval to [the practice of] purity...
King Bimbisāra and seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan were reborn together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).

The *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations* indicates that Vaidehī and five hundred handmaidens likewise beheld Amitābha. As for Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu in the eastern lands, as well as [Zhiyi of] Tiantai...
O Worthy One! Among the venerable masters of all schools, there are none who do not proclaim the practice of pure karma and collectively cultivate the Western Paradise.
How could their awakening and realization possibly fall below that of people today?
Question: It is indeed true that the Pure Land’s gathering of sentient beings is vast.

However, since the so-called Pure Land is located beyond ten trillion Buddha-lands, it seems to be merely attached to external traces when compared with the teachings of the "Pure Land of the Mind" and "Amitābha as one's own original nature."
Answer: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "From the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.
It further states: "The arising of all phenomena is manifested solely by the mind. How could there be a Buddha-land existing outside the mind?
One should know that there is no land outside the mind, and no mind outside the land. This refers to what are called the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions.
The land is none other than the land within my own mind. The Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the three periods of time are none other than the Buddhas within my own mind.
To know this is to know that there is not a single land that does not rely upon my mind for its establishment, and not a single Buddha who does not manifest due to my own nature.
If this is so, then how could the Ultimate Bliss beyond ten million *koṭis* of lands be anything other than the sole manifestation of my own mind?
The Pure Land—the Lord of the Land of Ultimate Bliss—is he not uniquely the Amitābha of one’s own original nature? Question:
The discourse on the Pure Land is likely a symbolic expression of the Dharma. A person of wisdom should directly awaken to the Zen school; only then can it be considered the superior approach.
If one merely extols the Pure Land, will this not lead to attachment to phenomenal forms and a failure to understand the principle of nature?
Answer: "The nature of returning to the source is non-dual; the expedient means have many gates.

If one understands this principle, then the Chan school and Pure Land are different paths leading to the same destination. As Grand Master Zhongfeng said: "Chan is the Chan of Pure Land; Pure Land is the Pure Land of Chan.
Although they are mutually elucidated, the practitioner must necessarily value entering deeply through a single gate. Therefore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta...

Upon reaching the stage of a Bodhisattva, one attains the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha) and says: "By means of the mind that mindfully recollects the Buddha, I shall enter the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva enters the inconceivable realm of liberation within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and says: "May I, at the time of my death, be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Thus, these two great beings—one serves as an attendant to the Teacher of this Sahā world, and the other serves as an attendant to the Guide of the Land of Utmost Bliss.
It is appropriate for each to establish its own gateway, yet they should be harmonized and integrated so that the two do not obstruct one another; how can you still cling to partial views?

Furthermore, when you say that the Pure Land symbolizes the Dharma, is it not because the pure mind itself is the Pure Land, such that there is no longer a need for a Pure Land adorned with the seven treasures?
If this is indeed the case, then you must also say that the virtuous mind itself is [the Pure Land].
Heaven need not necessarily consist of the Yāma or Trāyastriṃśa realms; an evil mind is itself hell—it need not necessarily involve swords, blades, boiling cauldrons, or hot water.
Ignorance is itself the realm of animals—it need not necessarily involve being covered in fur or wearing horns.

Thus, since the Pure Land of Quiescent Light exists, it can be known that there must necessarily exist lands such as the Land of True Reward and Adorned Lands. How much more so for those outside of these phenomena?

This is impossible. Apart from phenomena, there is no intrinsic nature. If you insist on abandoning phenomena to seek principle, or leaving phenomena to search for nature, then even the non-obstruction between principle and phenomenon cannot be achieved;
how then can you hope for the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena? Furthermore, although you possess the nature of a Tathāgata, [you have not yet realized it].
At present, you still possess the body of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). If you were truly able to regard every place as a pure land (*śuddhāvāsabhūmi*), tell me:
could you settle yourself amidst a latrine as if upon a mat? Could you eat from the same trough as dogs, pigs, oxen, and horses?
Can you lie down and sleep together with a rotting corpse being gnawed by maggots?

If you can do so, then feel free to say that high mountains and level plains are all the Western Land; feel free to say that even when encountering the "wind-sword" of death, one remains forever at ease.
If this is still not the case, then the views of impurity and purity have not yet been emptied, and feelings of love and hatred still remain;
yet you employ vast realms of experience to engage in grandiloquent talk, causing those of shallow insight to merely skim through a few volumes of scripture.
To merely glance at a few koans and immediately wish to slander the Dharma and commit transgressions—whose fault is this?
Question: One practices the Way seeking liberation from birth and death; therefore, the state of non-arising (anutpāda) is esteemed. Yet, one admires the Western Paradise and vows to go there;
would this not be contrary to the meaning of non-arising?
Answer: To take arising as arising is the error of the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). To take non-arising as non-arising is the delusion of the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
That which is arising yet non-arising, and non-arising yet arising, is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*):
its essence is fundamentally non-arising, yet through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the characteristic of arising appears; for the nature is capable of manifesting.
Because of these marks, it is said that non-arising is itself arising. Because marks manifest through nature, it is said that arising is itself non-arising.

To know this is to know that birth in the Pure Land is produced solely by the mind. If you doubt that it is distant and difficult to reach, consider that the mind encompasses the great void and its measure pervades the entire Dharma-realm; how could there be any distance?

Question: Among the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, those that are pure and sublime are many. Why is it that you now specifically point to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and furthermore, specifically praise its excellence of environment and excellence of conditions?
Answer: This land is a place where all manner of suffering converges; even if there are conditions for happiness, they invariably result in the fruit of suffering.
It is not so in the West. Therefore, a sutra says: "All these sentient beings have no manifold sufferings, but experience only various joys;

therefore, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī). Let us briefly compare the two lands. How could they possibly differ by anything less than heaven and earth? For instance, in this region, entering the womb is inevitably...

Having completed ten months in the womb, at the moment of birth, one dwells as a neighbor to spirits; they, however, take up residence within the lotus calyx, sitting peacefully in a palace of exquisite fragrance.
Thus, they are neither defiled by the impurities of the womb nor burdened by the arduous labors of their mother.

In the human world, the suffering of birth has already ceased; yet here, those who are elderly have white hair and wrinkled faces, with stooped waists and hunched backs, requiring assistance to sit or rise, their breaths faint and gasping.
Those [in the Pure Land], however, nourish their spirits with the flavor of the Dharma and shall never again suffer from aging or decay.
In the lands of the ten directions, they travel back and forth in a mere instant; thus, the suffering of old age in the human world is avoided.
When those in this world encounter even a single illness, they groan upon their beds, writhing and wailing in lamentation;

yet there, they possess great supernormal powers and great majesty, such that even the name of pain is unheard within their realms, and the suffering of sickness in the human world is utterly severed. As for the people of this world...
There must inevitably be death; with death, there must inevitably be transgression. One can only bow one's head and submit to bondage, being handed over to Yama.

Yet, by entrusting oneself once to the lotus-womb, one immediately attains a body of indestructible vajra, endowed with the marks and signs of excellence and radiant light, with immeasurable lifespan, and the suffering of human death is cast aside.
In this world, where union must inevitably be followed by separation, it is difficult for parents who have labored so hard...
In this world, husbands and wives bound by affection mostly end up separated;

yet those who are kin within the Dharma remain forever close to one another—how could they suffer the pain of being parted from loved ones? Here, enemies pursue one another, and grievances must inevitably be avenged.
Great terror cuts through the heart; there is no way to escape it. There, beings are affectionate and respectful toward one another, and none are not superior friends of a bodhisattva.
As they associate with one another, have they ever experienced the suffering of encountering those whom one hates?

Here in this world, human beings rush about for the sake of food and clothing, driven by their wives and children, enduring myriad forms of hardship. There, however, when one thinks of clothing, clothing arrives; when one longs for food, food comes forth.
The palaces and gardens are entirely composed of the seven treasures; each person enjoys them spontaneously, and has there ever been the suffering of lacking what one seeks?
It is not merely this: in this world, the physical body is ugly and defiled, with many faculties that are deficient or coarse;
in that land, the radiance is brilliant and magnificent, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence. In this world, beings emerge and submerge like a wheel, revolving through birth and death.
In that land, one realizes non-arising and never regresses; here in this world, there are only hills, mounds, pits, and ravines, with forests of thorns and brambles.
In that land, jewel-trees reach toward the heavens and the ground is made of gold. Furthermore, in this world, one merely looks up to the illustrious names of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
in that land, these two great Bodhisattvas personally serve as one’s supreme friends. When comparing the two, the contrast is evident.

The environment and conditions are exceptionally superior. As for the superiority of the environment, it can engender a pure mind; as for the superiority of the conditions, they can assist the power of one's practice.
Question: The mind of longing and aversion is precisely the thought of love and hatred. Love and hatred are matters pertaining to the shores of birth and death;
they are not appropriate for a practitioner. How should one deal with this?

Answer: One feels weary of and seeks to leave the Sahā world, while yearning for and admiring Sukhāvatī. Although this involves a mind of attachment and aversion, it is not the attachment and aversion of the mundane world;
rather, it is the attachment and aversion by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transform ordinary beings into sages.

If one were not weary of and sought to leave it, how could one escape this turbid world of Sahā? If one did not yearn for and admire it, how could one be born in this Lotus Land of Ultimate Bliss? Indeed, it is because...
Only through wearying detachment can one transform from the mundane; only through joyful aspiration can one achieve the state of a sage.
Question: Here in this world, food, drink, clothing, dwellings, and utensils must all depend on labor and effort before they can be utilized.
Question: What is the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss? Why is it that all matters pertaining to the enjoyment of blessings arrive spontaneously?
Answer: All matters pertaining to the enjoyment of blessings arise from the cultivation of merit. In the continent of Uttarakuru, food, drink, and clothing [all appear naturally].
If even these can be fully enjoyed as they manifest, how much more so the jewel-adorned pure land of Amitābha Buddha, replete with ten thousand blessings?
The *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* states: "This lecture hall and palace were originally without a creator, nor do they come from anywhere."
Because the great merit of that Buddha’s vows is so profound, beings are born there through spontaneous transformation (*upapāduka*).

Furthermore, it is said that in the Buddha-fields of other directions, all are entirely virtuous and there is no place for the commission of evil; therefore, their merits are likewise all spontaneous.

Next, there are worlds where those who do good predominate and those who do evil are few; in these, there is also spontaneous merit that does not depend upon cultivation or effort. As for this world...
In this realm, evil is extremely prevalent while goodness is extremely rare; therefore, people do not cultivate themselves. Things do not exist inherently. Question:
For those who attain rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha, at the time of death, they all see the Buddha and Bodhisattvas personally coming to welcome and guide them.
As the Sūtra says: "If one recites and maintains the Rebirth Mantra three hundred thousand times, Amitābha Buddha will always abide before them."

[The Buddha] said: "I shall protect this person. Even if those throughout the worlds of the ten directions were all to recite mantras and all seek to be guided by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, how could Amitābha Buddha possibly remain above everyone's heads to go forth and welcome them?"
Answer: Even the light of the sun and moon in the heavens is able to illuminate the world universally; one does not suffer from a lack of light.
How much more so, then, is this the case for the Buddha’s vows and supernatural powers?

Question: At the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva was manifestly seated at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), yet all the other bodhisattvas, despite exhausting their supernatural powers, were unable to see him.
Now, those who attain rebirth there are all ordinary beings of the mundane level; how is it that they are immediately able to see the Buddha?
Furthermore, as for the Buddha seen by them, is he not in fact no different from the Buddha seen by the bodhisattvas?
Answer: The characteristics of the Buddha are generally thus, yet what is perceived differs for each individual.
Those who first encounter him in the Western Land perceive no more than the coarse characteristics of the Buddha, such as the thirty-two marks and the eighty secondary signs.

As for the statement in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that the Tathāgata possesses a number of great person’s marks equal to the atoms within ten *avataṃsaka*-treasury world-oceans, it is likely not the case [for those at this initial stage].
The Great Bodhisattvas cannot perceive it. It is like the *sūdhā* food consumed by the various devas: within a single vessel, the colors and flavors are each distinct.
Or it is like a sick person and a healthy person tasting the same thing together; their perceptions of sweetness and bitterness are vastly different.
Thus, when the World-Honored One pressed the earth with his toe, the great trichiliocosm became entirely golden, yet [only he perceived it as such].
The Brahma King Śaṅkhapāda was able to see it, while others were all unaware. It is the same with the sacred realm of the Pure Land. Question:
Is it true that by reciting the Buddha’s name here, a single lotus flower immediately grows within the Western Seven-Jeweled Pond?
If one is diligent, the flower gradually grows larger; if one becomes indolent or regresses, the flower withers and falls away? Answer: It is so.
Answer: This is easy to clarify. It is like a great, bright mirror: whatever object comes before it, its reflection must necessarily appear.
For instance, the Jeta Grove pavilion in the city of Śrāvastī was composed of nothing more than silver and lapis lazuli;
yet, even within its walls, the affairs of the entire city could be reflected. How much more so, then, the pure and majestic adornments of Amitābha Buddha!
Is this not the precious land adorned by [Amitābha]? It is certainly beyond doubt that by reciting the Buddha’s name here, one will be born upon a lotus in that land.

Question: If one can attain non-retrogression even while being accompanied by karmic obstacles during rebirth, why do people not simply attend to their worldly affairs before life ends, and only begin to recite the Buddha’s name when they are on the verge of death?
Answer: This is a heterodox teaching. To harbor such a single thought is to bring much self-delusion; to utter such a single word is to lead many others astray.

When a wicked person attains rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha at the moment of death, it must be because they possessed roots of goodness from past lives and further encountered a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra);
thus, they have this rare opportunity at the end of life. Such a case is but one among ten thousand people—how could each [wicked person] possibly [attain rebirth]?
When a person approaches the end of life, do they all not have this fortunate opportunity? The *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) states:
"There are ten types of people in the world who, at the moment of death, are unable to practice the Buddha-remembrance (*nianfo*): first, those who may not encounter virtuous friends;

second, those whose bodies are entangled by karmic burdens and have no leisure for Buddha-remembrance; third, those who lose their speech due to a stroke; fourth, those who lose their minds through insanity; fifth, those who encounter water..."
Sixth, encountering jackals or wolves. Seventh, having one's roots of faith destroyed by evil friends. Eighth, dying suddenly from a stupor after overeating.
Ninth, perishing on the battlefield. Tenth, falling from a high cliff. If any one of these occurs, it becomes difficult to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Even if one dies of illness, at the moment the four elements separate, one cannot avoid the winds [of death].
When the body is dismembered by knives, one is terrified and panicked; how could there be leisure to settle the mind and recite the Buddha’s name?

Furthermore, if karmic conditions have not yet ended, worldly thoughts have not ceased, private affairs remain unsettled, or funeral matters are unattended, one may seek physicians and consult diviners, thereby disturbing the mind.
With children weeping and wives wailing, the ears are startled and overwhelmed; within the four seas of the heart, there is no longer any sense of direction. At such a time—
At such times, one seeks to practice mindfulness of the Buddha with composure and hopes for single-mindedness without distraction; yet, this is utterly impossible. Thus, the ancients said:
"If you wait until old age before practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, the solitary graves will mostly be those of the young. And it is further said:

"In ordinary times, when exhorting others to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, everyone says, 'I am too busy. Yet, when the moment of impermanence finally arrives, even the most busy person must cease all activity. Such is human life."
How much time is there in this world? While one is still neither old nor ill, one should immediately cast aside worldly attachments and attend to essential matters.
If one gains a single day’s passage of time, one should recite the Buddha’s name for that day; if one gains a single period of effort, one should cultivate pure karma for that period.
Otherwise, once one loses this human body, it will be difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas. How perilous!
Question: It is certainly unreasonable to wait until old age to practice. However, ordinary people are all caught within the net of worldly affairs;
there are matters they cannot cast aside. What is to be done?

Answer: A person in this world must inevitably face death; whether one practices [the Way] or not, none can escape it. Between falling into decline and ascending to transcendence, which would you prefer?
If one truly contemplates impermanence with deep sorrow, why worry that one’s application of mind will not be earnest?

Whether in stillness or in bustle, in favorable or adverse circumstances, reciting the Buddha’s name while seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is in no way obstructed by these conditions. Even if, in this world...

The conditions are extremely grave; you must also steal moments of leisure from amidst your busyness and establish this as a daily practice. Whether ten thousand or a thousand times, it must not be interrupted.
For those who are most preoccupied with affairs, the ten recitations at dawn must certainly not be omitted.
Question: It is said that by maintaining a single mind without distraction for one day up to seven days, one will attain rebirth.
If one maintains a single mind for within those one to seven days, but thereafter cannot maintain it, I do not know whether one can still attain rebirth.
Answer: Although one can maintain single-mindedness, the subsequent mind will inevitably become slightly distracted; yet, it will not reach the point of great distraction.

This is like Yan Hui, who did not deviate from benevolence for three months. During those three months, he was certainly a man of benevolence; but does that mean he suddenly became an evil person after the three months?
If you can constantly examine yourself and frequently make grand vows, there will be no [state] that cannot be produced.

Question: One who practices mindfulness of the Buddha must maintain a continuous succession of thoughts for their merit to become profound. However, during the summer months, one spends much time with the body bare.

How can one remain in full dress all day long? Furthermore, it is unknown how one should act regarding eating, drinking, sitting, or lying down, as well as when bathing or washing the mouth while naked.
"Is it permissible for all to recite the Buddha's name?
Answer: "There is no harm in silent recitation. This is what is meant by 'in moments of haste one must rely on this; in times of distress one must rely on this.
Question: When one is single-mindedly invoking the Name, yet also gives rise to the aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land, does this not seem like a confusion of two things?"
Question: How should one practice this? Answer:
Reciting the name is precisely the means for seeking rebirth. As the sutra says: "One should make a vow, wishing to be born in that land. It further states:
"To uphold the name" refers to a single matter, not two separate matters. This is analogous to those who prepare for the civil service examinations.

Those who desire to attain fame and achievement, and those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land—there seems to be a slight distinction between these two in their approach to reading, writing, and the recitation of the Name.

Consequently, when seeking rebirth, one should maintain a focused mind during the times of making vows at dawn and dusk, as well as at the moments of chanting the Name; one must not allow the mind to be distracted by other concerns.
Question: To practice mindfulness of the Buddha throughout the entire day and to perform meritorious deeds whenever one encounters them is indeed the fundamental duty of a student.

However, when performing such meritorious deeds, it is inevitable that the mind will be focused on the activity rather than the name of the Buddha. I do not know if this constitutes an obstacle to "single-mindedness without distraction."
Answer: A clear mirror is fundamentally empty; when objects come before it, they appear. What hindrance is there within the emptiness of the mirror?
People merely suffer from the illness of anticipating what has not yet arrived and lingering over what has already passed. This alone constitutes their affliction.

Question: The kindness of one's parents is most difficult to repay. If one can attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land, I do not yet know if there exists a method by which one may repay that debt of gratitude. Furthermore, in a single lifetime, one has but one set of parents;

yet across hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, one would have had hundreds of thousands of millions of parents. I wonder if, after attaining rebirth, one is able to remember each of them individually.
"Can one remember their names and recall each of their locations so as to report to them one by one?
He replied, "To wish to repay such virtue is like the vastness of Heaven—there is no limit to it. This is a worldly saying;

yet, using worldly ways to repay one's parents, there is truly no method by which one can fully repay them. However, if after rebirth one wishes to repay one's parents, then it becomes exceedingly easy."

Indeed. Not only can one repay the kindness of relatives of this single lifetime, but even if one wishes to repay the parents of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lifetimes prior, there is likewise a method for doing so.
For once a person reaches the Western [Pure Land], they will necessarily attain the supernatural power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), by which they can see the affairs of countless worlds;
they will necessarily attain the supernatural power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), by which they can hear [the sounds] of countless worlds.
Regarding the voice: he must possess the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*), being able to know the thoughts of all sentient beings;

he must attain the supernormal knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*), being able to know matters of death and rebirth throughout immeasurable kalpas—namely, that such-and-such a person was in such-and-such a place.
"Such is his name, such his clan, such his lineage, and such his village; I know every detail.
He can be made to do whatever I wish, and he will exhaust himself in repaying my kindness. How could there be any parental grace that cannot be requited?"
In the past, Mencius praised the filial piety of Shun, saying: "To be the father of the Son of Heaven is the height of honor;
to be nourished by the whole world is the height of sustenance. May I, in my future life, become a Bodhisattva, so that my parents may become the parents of a Bodhisattva.

Is this not more honorable than being among humanity? Furthermore, it allows one’s parents to be reborn in the Pure Land; when one thinks of clothing, clothing arrives, and when one imagines food, food appears.
Thus, they receive spontaneous blessings and enjoy infinite longevity—is this not far superior to nourishing them with the whole world?
Moreover, within a single realm, there can be no more than one Son of Heaven; if there were a second filial son, [the throne would be contested].

If one were to come forth [from seclusion] while still harboring the thought of nourishing oneself with the whole world, one would surely plot unlawful schemes and become a rebellious minister or a traitorous son.
How could this compare to the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, which allows all people to fully exercise their filial piety without obstructing the laws of the mundane world?
Question: "Sentient beings of different classes who undergo suffering within the three evil realms are infinite in number.
How could I possibly save them one by one? Why do you merely make such empty vows?"
Answer: A Bodhisattva who wishes to universally deliver sentient beings regards all those suffering within the three evil realms as people for whom he must provide salvation within his own domain.
How could he allow himself to feel fear because they are numerous, or to feel aversion or weariness because they are so many?
As the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha said: "If hell is not empty, I vow not to attain Buddhahood. Thus it is with Samantabhadra.
The ten great vows of a bodhisattva take the exhaustion of the realm of sentient beings as their ultimate limit.

That being so, those who cultivate pure karma and desire to be reborn in the Western Land should not vow to return to this Sahā world with the sole purpose of rescuing those in the three miserable realms. Is this not the case?

Question: Subtle life-forms are exceedingly numerous. Even if one were to give rise to the resolve for their rescue and deliverance upon seeing each such creature, would this resolve alone suffice to fulfill my aspiration? Or would it still be of benefit to them?
Answer: One should observe whether the sincerity of the aspiration is genuine. If one can exhaustively manifest such sincerity, there will be nothing that does not benefit others.

By observing the story of the World-Honored One in a past kalpa as the Rishi Kṣāntivādin and the story of Maudgalyāyana in a past kalpa as a woodcutter, one will know that the aspiration is beneficial.
Śākyamuni Tathāgata, in immeasurable kalpas ago, was the Rishi Kṣāntivādin.
While practicing the Way in the mountains, he encountered a king who had gone out hunting. Pursuing a fleeing beast, the king asked the practitioner, "Where is this animal going now?
At that moment, if he had told the truth, the animal would have been harmed; yet if he had not told the truth, it would have been a lie. He hesitated, unable to respond.

The king grew angry and lopped off one of his arms. When he questioned him again, the practitioner remained silent and did not answer; so the king lopped off his other arm as well. The practitioner then made a vow, saying:
"After I have attained Buddhahood, I shall first deliver this man, lest people of the world follow his example in committing evil.
Later, the very first person he delivered was the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya, who was none other than the king of that time. Thus it is said in the *Buddhacarita*.
There was a city whose people were difficult to convert. The Buddha said, "These people have a karmic affinity with Maudgalyāyana.

He therefore dispatched him there, and the people indeed all turned toward conversion. They asked the Buddha about the causal conditions for this, and the Buddha said: "In a past kalpa, Maudgalyāyana was once a woodcutter."
Countless chaotic bees were startled into flight. Maudgalyāyana admonished them, saying: "You all possess Buddha-nature.
In the future, when I have attained the Way, I shall come to deliver you. These people of this city today are none other than those bees of that day;

because they once gave rise to a single thought, they share a karmic affinity with me. Contemplating this, one sees that it is not only among all human beings that one should exhort others [to seek awakening].

When one practices mindfulness of the Buddha and gives rise to the thought of rescuing and delivering others, one should immediately perceive that all beings of different species should likewise, on their behalf, practice mindfulness of the Buddha and give rise to the thought of rescuing and delivering them.
Question: Although the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is sincere, the number of recitations is limited.

Even if one were to offer a thousand recitations of the Buddha’s name for the sake of a hundred lives, those hundred lives would naturally partake of its merit; what need then be said of the myriad beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
Furthermore, if one bestows the merit by chanting the Buddha’s name a thousand times, the resulting blessing becomes increasingly slight.

Why is this so? The answer is: it is like a single torch; if a hundred people divide it among themselves, the torch remains as it was. Even if a thousand or ten thousand people divide it, the torch remains just as it was.
Question: In the past, there were two monks who, during their practice of *nien-fo*, visualized themselves sitting within a great lotus flower.
They cultivated the visualization of the lotus opening and closing in this manner for five months and both attained rebirth [in the Pure Land].
I do not know whether practitioners of *nien-fo* may take this as a standard procedure.
Answer: It is so. Ultimately, mindfulness of the Buddha is the primary practice.
