*The Direct Instruction for Returning West*, Scroll Three.
Compiled by the Layman of Huaixi, Zhou Mengyan (Anshi), of Yufeng;
printed by the Layman of Shenglian, Luo Wanzhong (Yunmei), of Loudong. *Quanshen qixin zashuo* (Exhortations for Awakening Faith:
Miscellaneous Discourses).
To exhort those of great wisdom with the teaching of the Pure Land is very easy to transform and guide, for their past merit is profound and their faculties are extraordinary.
To exhort foolish men and women with the teaching of the Pure Land is likewise easy to transform and guide, for they lack preconceived notions;
they are like sweet things that can accept blending, or white things that can accept dyeing.
I have gathered these words to guide the lost and lead them back to faith. It is indeed not easy to convey such teachings to us who have studied the books;
for we are already bound by a layer of superficial clichés that remain firmly fixed within our minds.

Consequently, even when the ultimate Way is present, we have no desire to hear it, and even when there are excellent words, we have no desire to listen. Thus, I have compiled this "Guiding the Lost Back to Faith."
Regarding the statement, "That which can be used to illuminate the Pure Land," I have excerpted several passages to serve as a source of Dharma-joy,
titled *Miscellaneous Discourses for Inspiring Faith*.
This is the "Exhortation to Practice" by the Layman Ruru, Yan Bing.
Everyone cherishes this physical body, yet who believes that the body is the root of suffering? Moment by moment they crave pleasure, unaware that such joy is the cause of future pain.
This ephemeral life is easily passed; how could it be a place for long-term dwelling? This illusory form is not solid; it all returns to annihilation.
Those who live long may only reach eighty or ninety before they perish; those with short lives do not even last two or three decades before they die young.

Furthermore, there are those who know nothing of today, let alone what tomorrow holds. There are also those who, while still on their bed, suddenly bid farewell, or who leave their shoes by the bedside.
In a mere breath’s time, one is gone; then it is a parting for all eternity. To sigh that this body has no place of permanence—what can one do? Who can help?
Do not be deceived by it. It is but seven feet of sinews wrapped around bones, and a bundle of flesh encased in skin.

Hair, fur, nails, and teeth are heaped together like dust; tears, mucus, and saliva are as filthy as a public latrine. In winter’s cold and summer’s heat, one year after year lives a precarious life amidst malaria;
bitten by lice and pierced by mosquitoes, year after year one passes the time mingling with maggots. This body is nothing but...
How can those who are deluded still display such elegance? How can these ignorant fellows still harbor such perversions?
Some pin flowers or grass upon their skull-like heads; others carry musk and incense at the side of their stinking skin-sacks.
Silk robes completely shroud bags of pus and blood; brocade coverlets entirely conceal buckets of excrement and urine. To what end do they exhaust themselves?

With a hundred schemes born of a treacherous heart, one thinks they shall dwell in this world for ten thousand years; yet one knows not that the head will ache and the eyes grow dim, until the King Yama receives the person and leads them away.
Furthermore, as the temples turn white and the teeth fall out, the Ghost of Impermanence sends word to seek them out. Every individual clings to sensual pleasures and covets wealth;
these are all swift paths to losing one's human form. Day after day indulging in wine and craving meat is nothing other than planting the seeds [of future suffering].
The deep-rooted foundation of hell lies in seeking fleeting pleasure before one's eyes while enduring bitter suffering for ten thousand kalpas thereafter.
Once the life-roots are severed and the four elements are sliced by the knives of the winds, externally the limbs are pulled apart, and internally the liver and intestines tear with pain.
Even if one’s wife and children cherish you, there is no way to detain you; even if one’s own flesh and bones fill one’s sight, who can...

For your sake, those who remain alive lament in vain with piercing grief; as for the deceased, they merely perceive their consciousness rushing forward, seeing no light ahead and finding no companion upon raising their eyes.
Upon crossing the Nai River, there is none who beholds this and does not feel sorrow.

Entering the Pass of the Ghost Gate, those who arrive naturally feel a sense of profound sorrow. Having departed this world for only seven days, one is cast into the underworld and gradually passes through the various offices.
There, the officials clutch their ledgers, devoid of human feeling; the jailers hold their pitchforks, their faces never smiling.

Those who practiced virtue throughout their lives are sent back to the Way of the Gods or the Way of the Immortals; those who committed evil while alive are driven into the realms of boiling water and blazing fire.

Regarding "Swords and Ointment": At first, everyone said that cause and effect were but empty delusions; only now do we know that these words are not false. Within the mirror of retribution, every detail is laid bare;
within the dark chambers of the underworld, there is every kind of bitter suffering. On the mountains of swords and trees of blades, one endures ten thousand varieties of torment;
with horns upon one's head and fur upon one's back, one cannot repay the karmic debts of many lifetimes. No matter how heroic your heart or how bold your spirit may be—
One cannot help but bow one's head before the ghost-wardens; though they may slander the Way and disparage the monks, one cannot avoid kneeling before Lord Yama.
Although the soul has returned to the realm of the dead, the physical corpse still lies within the coffin.
After three or five days have passed, or during the sixth or seventh month, it becomes putrid and rots, emitting worms and blood, and its foul stench permeates the earth.
The smoke rises to the heavens. Those without wealth are consigned to a single heap of wild fire;
those with status and reputation are buried in desolate mountains ten thousand *li* away. That once-lovely, rosy countenance has turned to ashes;
today’s desolate white bones have become mere dust. Former affections have here reached emptiness; where are the heroes of old now? Only green grass...
At the edge, the stele and stone remain; within the green willows, paper-money hangs empty. When one contemplates reaching the final conclusion at the very tip, who can avoid such a fate?
If you wish to leap out of saṃsāra, you must turn your heart toward perfect enlightenment. Do not seek a livelihood within the ghost cave;
you must know that the True Person resides upon the flesh-ball of the body. Whether male or female, all are capable of cultivation. If...
Whether layperson or monastic, all have their allotted portion. In seeking a way to survive in this urgency, you must contemplate the body after death; do not hesitate or turn back.

This life is originally but a dream within a dream. If you wait for tomorrow until tomorrow comes again, look at how you will waste your youth, causing future generations to grieve for you as they did for those before, piling up white bones in endless succession. Recite the name of Amitābha well; do not let that land remain empty.
The Golden Terrace; Old Yan is heartless—do not provoke his iron staff. Abandon evil and follow good; reform the past and cultivate the future.
Proclaim this before the assembly for the sake of the great multitude; explain it upon returning home for the sake of one’s family. Cause all who encounter it to simultaneously attain awakening;
teach every person to together avoid sinking into the depths of delusion. If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be believed? Thus says the Way-man.
Do not practice other paths; they are difficult to cultivate. Each of you should directly take responsibility for your own realization. Do not let this life pass in vain.

The obstruction of principle is even more severe than the arising of desire, like a blind person who does not recognize an elephant. There was once a king who gathered a group of blind men and asked them: "You all..."

He wished to know whether they could discern the form of the elephant. They all replied, "We wish to know. He then ordered an elephant-handler to lead the elephant into the courtyard and summoned the group of blind men to feel it with their hands.
Once they had finished feeling it, he asked, "Have you now discerned the form of the elephant? They all replied, "We have discerned it."
Thereupon, each made his own conjecture. He who felt its trunk said, "The elephant's form is like a lute. He who felt its legs said, "The elephant's form is like pillars.
He who felt its back said, "The elephant's form is like a house. He who felt its flanks said, "The elephant's form is like walls.
He who felt its ears said, "The elephant's form is like winnowing baskets. He who felt its tail said, "The elephant's form is like brooms. Thus they spoke, each [according to what he touched].
Each adhered to their own interpretation, disputing without end and eventually resorting to physical blows. The king laughed and said, "None of you truly know the elephant.
The lute is its trunk; the pillars are its feet; the roof is its back; and the walls are its flanks."
The winnowing basket was its ears; the broom was its tail. Consequently, the group of blind men remained silent and did not dare speak.

Nevertheless, in their minds they still believed what they had felt by touch was not erroneous, yet they harbored a great resentment that all the others' descriptions were wrong. Thus, throughout their lives, these blind men never truly knew the form of the elephant.
Had they not been instructed to feel it with their hands, then the shape of the elephant would have remained [unknown] beyond a few words.
Thus one understands why there comes to be such contention. It is simply because they possess this single "impression" (mō);
they then claim to have personally verified it with their own hands and are free from all doubt. Consequently, they hold fast to it within their hearts so firmly that it cannot be uprooted.
As for those who do not read books, if they are taught to cultivate the Pure Land, even if they cannot all believe it, they will certainly not go so far as to slander it. If...
Upon reading the first book on the imperial examinations, one immediately considers oneself correct;

with an empty stomach and a haughty mind, one regards these as nothing more than the teachings of the Buddhists, treating their sincere words as absurdities and viewing the pouring of nectar as the consumption of poison.
Therefore it is said that the obstruction of intellectual principles is even more severe than that of desire.
First, one must understand the doctrine of the three periods of time.
There are those among scholars who do not believe in past and future lives; because of this, they do not believe in the Pure Land.
This is because they do not realize that past and future lives are simply yesterday and tomorrow—they exist inherently from the very beginning and were not fabricated by the Buddha. For example:
The five viscera and six bowels originally reside within the patient's own abdomen;

how can it be that because they have emerged from the mouths of physicians, one consequently regards them as mere items in a medicinal basket? In the "Exhortation to Students" by Lord Wenchang, he says at the outset:
"I have been a scholar-official for seventeen lifetimes," which clearly establishes that there are three [past] lives.
The titles and honors of the scholar-officials have all passed through his administration; how could his words not be trusted?
Furthermore, one must clarify the principle of cause and effect.
That Confucianists do not believe in cause and effect is not a lack of faith in Buddhism, but rather a lack of faith in Confucianism itself. The *I Ching* says: "Accumulation..."
In the house of those who do good, there will surely be an abundance of blessings. In the house of those who accumulate non-good, there will surely be an abundance of calamities.
The Book says: "For doing good, a hundred auspicious signs descend upon them; for doing non-good, a hundred calamities descend upon them. Now, doing good and doing non-good are the causes;

the descending of auspicious signs and the descending of calamities are the effects. It is like the moon and the sun: they are one and the same substance. Therefore it is said that if you wish to know—
What was caused in a previous life is what one receives in this life. If people believe this teaching, they will naturally dare not commit evil.
Should they regard retribution as a mere absurdity, they will fall into deceiving and cheating others without any sense of restraint.
Furthermore, within a single district, if one person believes it and performs one act of goodness, ten thousand people will increase their store of ten thousand good deeds. One...
If one person acts out a single evil deed without belief [in its consequences], ten thousand people will consequently increase their evils by ten thousandfold. Therefore it is said:
"When everyone believes in cause and effect, it is the way to great order; when no one believes in cause and effect, it is the way to great chaos."
The principle of the three periods of time must have been spoken of by Confucius;

the doctrine of the three periods is attested in the classics and histories, where it is recorded in great abundance. Even in the worldly experiences and observations of today, such matters are not uniform.
Yet, scholars refrain from speaking of it simply because Confucius never explicitly mentioned it. However, [this does not mean it is untrue].

How could it be that there was anything Confucius did not speak of? If one were to claim that Confucius was ignorant of the three periods of existence (the *triloka*), he could no longer be considered a sage.
Within the entire *Lunyu*, the words spoken by Confucius amount to no more than eight thousand five hundred and three characters;
thus, there must have been much that he spoke which has not been transmitted to posterity. If one insists on waiting for it to appear in the extant scriptures...
Only then can one believe [the following]: within the Four Books and Five Classics, Confucius never spoke of his own parents;
thus, a Confucian should also keep his own birth concealed and never speak of it. He never spoke of his brothers; thus, a Confucian should not mention his siblings.
He never spoke of his house, fields, or lands; thus, a Confucian should not dwell in palatial residences.
"Professionally produced [ink] is constantly available. It is not merely that these 'Four Treasures of the Study' have never been mentioned in the Classics;
your practice of calligraphy is flawed. Beyond the rule of wearing hemp in summer and furs in winter, there has never been mention of undergarments.
Could it be that those who wear trousers today are not acting contrary to this? Gold and tin from Jiangnan are not things a Confucian scholar ought to employ, nor are the pigments of Western Shu."
One should not apply such colorful rhetoric. Why? Because Confucius never uttered such words from his own mouth; they are merely what has been transmitted through the scriptures.
Confucius taught people filial piety and fraternal duty, yet the Confucian scholars are unwilling to practice filial piety and fraternal duty.

He taught people loyalty and reciprocity, yet the Confucian scholars are unwilling to practice loyalty and reciprocity. He never encouraged people to gamble, yet the Confucian scholars are particularly fond of gambling. And so forth...
He has never been taught to do this or that, yet he insists on doing this or that. Why is this so?
To summarize it in a single word: it is simply a lack of reflection.

The wise person should not regard their human existence as short-lived, for from the very beginning there has never been such a thing as death. The name "death" is derived solely from the physical body;

while the physical body undergoes change and transformation, our fundamental nature is inherently without change. It is like a traveler on a long journey who may ride in a boat or sit in a sedan chair.
Whether it be galloping horses or driving carriages, boats, carts, palanquins, or steeds—these are the physical body. Those who ride in boats, carts, palanquins, or on horses are the true nature.
Speaking in terms of the physical body, its duration does not exceed a hundred years; yet if one speaks of my original face, how could it be anything less than as vast as heaven and earth?
Reflecting quietly upon this, what joy there is! As for those today who do not believe in the afterlife:
They recognize the existence of the physical body but fail to recognize the true nature; this is to regard oneself as clearly destined for a short life.
This, too, is a delusion of perception.
A person of wisdom must not narrow their scope of knowledge and experience.
Within the mental vision of a farmer, he does not know the realm of a wealthy man; within the mental vision of a wealthy man, he does not know the realm of an emperor.

Though they share the same status as human beings, the difference between them is vast. How much more so when one proceeds from humanity to the celestial realm, and further from the celestial realm to the Buddha-land!
It is said that those who study the classics must possess broad knowledge and experience; yet how could one know this?

The more one is a scholar who reads books, the narrower their见闻 (what they have seen and heard) becomes; this is because they cling tenaciously to what was first introduced to them, remaining firm and unshakable.

For what such a person has seen and heard does not extend beyond this single land, and they do not know that worlds are manifold and inexhaustible, nor that suns and moons are manifold and likewise inexhaustible; they know only of their own initial birth.

As for the people, they began with Pangu. It is unknown how many kalpas have passed since the Great King Samatā-vijaya first established [this land], but it is already the ninth minor kalpa of the present era.

We know only that this place is called Zhonghua (the Central Kingdom), yet we do not realize that within the single continent of Jambudvīpa, there are already sixteen great nations, five hundred middle kingdoms, and one hundred thousand small states that call themselves Zhonghua.
In small countries, people know only that when one reaches seventy years of age, it is called "the age of rare attainment" (guxi).

They do not know that at the beginning of the kalpa, human lifespans all began at eighty-four thousand years. They know only that the source of clothing and food in this region must come from agriculture and sericulture;

they do not know that in the celestial palaces and Buddha-lands, garments arrive as soon as they are thought of, and food appears as soon as it is imagined. They know only gold, silver, and precious treasures.
This region is extremely difficult to encounter. One does not know that the great earths of the Buddha-lands in the ten directions are all composed of the seven treasures;

one merely sees the written characters of this region, which consist only of the Six Scripts created by Cang Jie. One does not know that since the beginning of creation, there have already been sixty-four types of calligraphy;
yet, knowing only the minor classics such as the *Zuo Zhuan*, *Guo Yue*, *Shiji*, and *Hanshu*, one immediately claims to be an artist of letters.
The foremost of gardens. One does not know that upon the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*), secret scriptures in lapis lazuli cases are piled as high as mountains;
one only knows that the human fleshly body must be formed from the semen and blood of a man and a woman.

One does not know that this substance may be entrusted to a lotus-womb, born in a place of supreme, wondrous fragrance and purity, such that it need not pass through a woman’s belly. One only knows that one has obtained a spouse.
A woman who is yellowish and emaciated is then loved, cherished, treasured, and doted upon; she alone is listened to when she speaks.
Yet how could one know that when a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) reigns, in addition to the Jade Woman (Apsaras), there are still twenty thousand exquisite ladies?
As for the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the number of his Jade Women is reckoned in the tens of billions. For each single Jade Woman—

On the side, he transformed himself into a celestial king to provide him with entertainment. [The king] knew only that humans are the most spiritual among all things, and believed they could assist in the transformation and nourishment of the world and participate in the workings of Heaven and Earth;

he did not know that humanity is but one of the six realms of existence, one of the four modes of birth, and one of the ten dharma-realms. He knew only to serve and obtain the rank of one or two sages.
A person might then claim that their own master is peerless and supreme, while all other gods, spirits, earth deities, humans, and ghosts are unworthy of belief;
they would dismiss every matter never witnessed by their own eyes as mere fantasy.

How could they know that within each and every land there are several sages presiding over and teaching the transformation of beings? Among the vast multitude of humanity within Jambudvīpa, there are in total six...
There are fourteen hundred such types. It is not that sages exist only in this one place alone. Alas!
How could those who pursue fame, beauty, wealth, and profit ever perceive even a fraction of such a realm?

They are like earthworms, which know only the pleasure of feeding on mud within a span of a foot of soil, yet remain ignorant of the azure dragon leaping in the great ocean amidst surging waves and crashing billows. It is just like this.
The dung beetle knows only the joy of rolling balls of filth within the manure; it does not know that the great Peng soars ninety thousand li upon the winds that blow beneath it.
Therefore, those who study the Buddha-dharma must open their eyes wide.
The Tripitaka must not fail to be read.
Fowl, dogs, cattle, and sheep can crow, bark, bellow, and low, yet they cannot speak; compared to those who are able to speak, the ability to speak renders humans noble.
A person who does not recognize a single character may still be able to speak with their mouth, yet they cannot speak with their hands.
Regarding speech: one who has mastered even a few characters can use the pen to communicate across a distance of a thousand *li*. Thus, one who has mastered even a few characters is precious.

Although such a person can use their hand to act as their mouth, they can never transform one hand into hundreds or thousands of hands, nor can they preserve that hand for hundreds or thousands of years. If, however, one could... [be extensive]... then [it would be different].

One who masters both the ancient and the modern, and composes works to bequeath to posterity, is able to have a single book printed as hundreds or thousands of copies, and for that single book to endure for hundreds or thousands of years.
Is such a person not most noble? Nevertheless, this is still merely a worldly book.
If, beyond the Confucian classics, one can further read extensively from the Buddhist canon, then throughout all the heavens above and the earth below, across past kalpas and future...
From the kalpas of the past to the dragon palaces and the oceanic treasuries, one can roughly grasp their general outlines; is not what has been seen and heard already extensive?

Nevertheless, though one’s见闻 (what is seen and heard) may indeed be vast, if one does not obtain the method of the shortcut to transcend the three realms, then one still has no share in the seeds of Bodhi.
However, if one can become broadly proficient in the Tripiṭaka and further encounter the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, and is able to be earnest...
Believe in them and practice them accordingly; this is the source from which merit and wisdom arise, and it is not a matter of merely three or five lifetimes.
Someone might say: "Though the texts of the Dragon Palace and the Sea Treasury are the sincere words of the Tathāgata, what can be done about the fact that Confucian scholars do not believe them?
I reply: If one were to inform them of the deeds of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, [they would likewise find them difficult to accept].
Those who are illiterate would likewise consider this preposterous. Therefore, Buddhist scriptures truly must be read.
Master Xuanzang was exceptionally skilled at providing such inspiration.
In the secular world, some may disparage the Sangha because they lack virtuous conduct and thus fail to believe in the Pure Land; this is an error.
It is like a base Daoist who, because of his own unworthiness, slights Laozi, or a base scholar who, because of his own unworthiness, slights Confucius.
A wise person does not reject the words because of the person; how much less could one slight a teaching because of its followers? As the Tang Emperor Taizong once said:
Dharma Master Xuanzang said, "Your Majesty wishes to provide a vegetarian feast for the Sangha, yet I have heard that many among the monks lack virtuous conduct; what can be done about this?
The Emperor replied, "In Kunshan there is jade, yet it is mixed with sand and silt. In the waters of Li there is gold, yet how could there not be shards and rubble?

A stone statue of an Arhat, carved from wood or earth, brings forth blessings if one treats it with reverence. A golden countenance cast from copper or iron incurs sin if one destroys it. It is the same with clay."
"Although a dragon cannot bring rain, one must pray to a clay dragon when seeking rain. Although an ordinary monk cannot bestow blessings, one must respect an ordinary monk when cultivating merit.
Emperor Taizong said with sudden realization, "From this day forward, even if I see a small novice monk..."
It was as if he were honoring the Buddha. Alas! Emperor Taizong truly possessed the merit of past lives; with a single stroke, he was awakened.
One may say that Master Xuanzang was also exceptionally skillful at providing inspiration.
One should cultivate a mind of weary detachment toward this physical body.
While a person lives in this world, they are tormented by the eight sufferings; yet, unaware of their own suffering, they instead regard it as pleasure.
It is only right that they enter from suffering into further suffering, with no end in sight. To speak of the suffering of birth: while a person dwells within the mother’s womb...
Below the liver and diaphragm, above the large intestine, it forms from the membranes like a blister, gradually taking shape. Enclosed within the womb, it cannot move freely.
When the mother eats hot food, it is as if she were pouring boiling water over it; when the mother drinks cold water, it is as if she were lying on ice.
The place where one dwells is utterly impure; that which one consumes consists entirely of unclean blood.

While residing in the womb, the period does not exceed three hundred days, yet the suffering endured is equivalent to many decades. Upon reaching full term, the body is inverted and suspended head-down toward the birth canal.
As the physical form gradually grows larger, there is no means by which to emerge; the path to self-destruction lies in this very moment.

It is carved; the mechanism for killing the mother is also contained within this single moment. At this time, the mother pulls it from the womb, and the pain is as if she were being torn apart by chariots.
For this reason, once it emerges from the womb, there is no one who does not let out a great cry. After emerging from the womb, excrement and urine are left in a state of utter disorder.
They do not know shame. It is the same with those who are called great in wealth and status; it is the same with those who are called great sages and worthies.

People merely habituate themselves to these things as a matter of course, and thus remain unaware and unawakened. If one could reflect upon this for a single clear night, would it not be a cause for sorrow and shame?
The Tathāgata, the Great Sage, out of compassion for the world, teaches people to seek rebirth [in the Pure Land].

In the Pure Land, one is born by transformation from a lotus flower, thereby escaping such calamities and hardships. Alas, how can you remain so deeply attached and immersed in defilement, failing to give rise to a sense of weary detachment?
A person of great filial piety does not wish to enter a womb.
When the divine consciousness enters the womb, not only does the individual suffer, but the mother likewise endures great agony.
Throughout the ten months in the womb, each day passes as if it were a year. Upon the moment of birth, the mother’s suffering takes myriad forms, a state of shame and dread beyond words.
Moment by moment she dwells as a neighbor to ghosts; in every thought she seeks life but cannot find it. Fortunately, this ordeal...
Life passes by in haste; one then cherishes an infant as if it were a treasure. Consequently, one pushes aside the dry bedding to lie upon the damp, caring for and lifting the child.
Much of the vital essence and blood of a lifetime is consumed in secret. Long ago, there was a seven-year-old śrāmaṇera who left the household life and attained the Way.
He recalled his past lives and sighed, saying: "My single body has caused five mothers to suffer grief and distress.
When we were mother and son for the first time, my neighbor was also born; I alone met an early death, and when my mother saw her neighbor’s child grow up, she immediately gave rise to sorrow.
When we were mother and son for the second time, I again died young; if my mother saw others nursing their infants, she would immediately give rise to grief."
When we were mother and son for the third time, he died at the age of ten; seeing other children eating and drinking like himself, his mother gave rise to grief and distress.
When we were mother and son for the fourth time, he died before marriage; seeing his peers taking wives, his mother gave rise to grief and distress.
Now, in this fifth life, he has left home at the age of seven; as my mother remembers him, she again gives rise to grief and distress.
I contemplate the cycle of birth and death; my accumulated kin have been like this. This is why I practice the Way with such diligence.

Today, among these people on the streets who pass by one another shoulder to shoulder in an unending stream, for the most part, many leave a burden upon their parents, while those who can repay their parental kindness are but few.
Indeed, in one lifetime spent in the womb, one burdens two parents; thus, in a hundred lifetimes, one would burden two hundred parents.
To leave behind one’s parents for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes is a heavy burden.
If one can transcend the mundane world and be born through transformation within a lotus flower, one will never again burden one’s parents forever; is this not the greatest of great filial piety?
Yet those who slander the Buddha today claim instead that leaving home is unfilial; they are thus content to remain perpetually in the womb, thereby burdening their parents.
This is what it means to be a true relative.
Great nobles must know how to feel shame;
for those called "noble" are not defined by the dignity of their rank or the prominence of their station, nor by possessing the five carriages of learning. It refers to one who is able—
"To depart from" refers to base behaviors. It means being able to abandon those base behaviors shared with birds and beasts.

Wherein does this baseness lie? It is said: greed, lust, killing, and theft; these are they. These are what birds and beasts share in common. Beyond these, there is yet another thing more shameful and loathsome than anything else:
namely, the matter of digesting excrement within the belly. This is true regardless of whether the food consists of rare delicacies or a hundred flavors.
Once it has entered the throat, it becomes one with the saliva, spittle, and brain-fluids, and flows downward along with them.
Within the stomach, there are yellow, elongated worms that coil, stretch, and writhe inside; after a full day and night, they bore into and devour the food, which then flows into the large intestine.
Its stench is unbearable to approach. As it accumulates in great quantities, it eventually surges forth through separate paths via the anus and the urethra, appearing loathsome and foul.
Their appearance is identical to that of dogs and pigs. Such base behavior, even if committed only once, is already shameful; how can one endure it day after day?
If one possesses such base conduct yet remains unaware of it and seeks no detachment from it, then one is no different from birds and beasts.
Therefore, one must surely reproach oneself and reform, desiring at every moment to cast off this base nature; only then is one truly noble.
Among these six heavens, although they partake of the heavenly *sudarśana* flavor, it is fragrant, pure, light, and clear, devoid of even the slightest speck of dust or dregs.

Fragrant clouds well forth from their bodies with sovereign ease. They traverse hundreds of thousands of millions of lands in an instant, coming and going without tears, phlegm, saliva, or the impurities of excrement and urine.
Therefore, a single fingernail of a celestial being is worth [the entire realm of] Yama.
Although one may dwell upon the land of Jambudvīpa, one cannot be called a person of great nobility so long as one is not yet exempt from the cycle of saṃsāra.
Only by transcending the mundane world and being born through transformation within a lotus can this state of lowliness be forever severed.
This is not something that the power of Confucius or Mencius can save me from.

The metaphor of the silkworm cocoon refers to the silkworm’s making of its cocoon. Having already moved it to the left and the right, and above and below, it exhausts everything within its belly to complete it;
only then does it presume to dwell permanently within it, believing itself to be safe and unharmed. How could it know why?
Those who manage their own affairs and pursue their own interests are merely entangling and binding themselves.

How could they know that others rely on what they have spat out to protect themselves, while people use what they have spat out to bring about their own destruction? There are tens of thousands, even millions, of such deluded insects.
Who can escape the boiling cauldron? Yet, in that place, fathers pass it on to their sons, and sons pass it on to their grandsons, entering the boiling cauldron;
thus, there is no suffering more惨烈 (cān-lè) than this. It is like the silkworm cocoons within the two great gates of the world.
It is exactly like this. Exhausting a lifetime of toil, one strives solely for the sake of providing food and clothing for wife and children;
one employs every stratagem and incurs every enmity, leaving no means untried. By the time the family estate is roughly established, this very body has already been bound within its constraints.
Among the tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of deluded people, who can escape the cycle of retribution? Yet they continue to raise their children...
Furthermore, it is transmitted from father to son, and from grandson to grandson, as a means of requital and retribution. Thus, nothing is more extraordinary than this.
As the *Sutra of Forty-two Sections* says: "A person's attachment to wife, children, and home is even greater than that of a prison.
While there is a time for release from prison, there is no thought of separation from one's wife and children."
The metaphor of the basket is like a fisherman who sets a basket in midstream to prevent fish from passing through.
He floats water plants alongside it to give the appearance of a place where they can hide, while secretly burying beneath the grass a basket that allows entry but not exit. Thereupon, the fish—

They scramble to cast themselves into it, thinking they can find refuge and support therein, unaware that they have already entered the basket. It is just like the net and curtain within the River of Desire.
People only perceive that when they are free from illness and affliction, their homes are secure and their wives and children are a reliable support;
thus they pass their time aimlessly and indifferently, neither perceiving nor understanding. Suddenly, the basket of Old Yama rises up, and—
Those whom one loves most—sons and fathers, husbands and wives—are each recorded in the registers and summoned away.
To contemplate this, how can it not be lamentable? Yet mere lamentation is of no avail; the only superior strategy is to ensure they do not dare to summon them.
Regarding the parable of the horse, there are four types of horses. The most excellent and noble horse gallops at the mere sight of the shadow of the whip, without waiting for being spurred.

Next is that which runs as soon as it is struck once by the whip. Further down is that which does not run when the whip is light, but only runs when the whip is heavy. And the lowest type is the dull-witted hack.
If a whip is heavy, one will not run away; only when the awl pierces the skin does the pain become so extreme that one finally flees.
It is the same for human beings: those who possess wisdom are easily awakened. Upon hearing within a hundred *li* that someone has died, one should immediately be struck with alarm, thinking:
"Within a hundred *li* someone has died; I too am a human being, and death will surely reach me. One must then practice with all haste to seek liberation.
These are those who gallop upon seeing the shadow of the whip. Next are those who awaken upon seeing a relative die.

Even further down are those who awaken after seeing a neighbor die. If one waits until one’s own old age or until one is personally ill before awakening, one is already like someone who only runs when the awl has pierced the skin. Should one still not [awaken] even in old age...
Awakening—or perhaps having fallen ill yet still failing to awaken—is this not equivalent to being no better than the wild fox?
The parable of the wild fox tells how a wild fox entered the kitchen at night, ate his fill, and fell asleep; when dawn broke, he was unable to escape and thus feigned death.
Yet it waited for others to abandon it. Before long, there was indeed one who wished to discard it. One person said, "The fox's tail is quite fine;
I shall wait until I have cut it off before I abandon you. Hearing this, the fox was terrified; enduring the pain, it allowed itself to be cut.
Suddenly, a young boy came, wishing to take its two ears. Hearing this, the fox became even more afraid, yet it reflected that its two ears were still unrelated to its essential nature.
He was ordered to do so, yet he continued to endure it. Suddenly, another person said, "The skin can be used to patch a fur robe.
The fox was greatly terrified and said, "If they take my skin, it will surely lead to my head being severed and my belly ripped open; how could this be endured?
Thereupon, he sprang up with vigor and fled wildly toward the outside, and the fox eventually escaped. Humans within the prison of the three realms are no different from those in a kitchen. Karma...

Having already been conceived in a womb as a human being, one can hardly escape the certainty of death. Only by reciting the Buddha’s name to attain rebirth in the Pure Land can one escape from the jaws of death.

Having missed the time of physical vigor, the fox-tail has already been cut off. If one reaches the twilight years of the setting sun, it will be too late—already like having one's head severed or one's belly ripped open.
Unless one establishes great vows and exerts oneself with reckless disregard for one's own body, how could one possibly succeed?
Leaping out of the path of delusion, one is received by the Buddha’s guidance.

Blaming the King of Darkness alone for their death, they appear before him and, according to their misdeeds, undergo punishment. The person says: "If I had known this would happen earlier, Great King, why..."
"Without first having passed through a single sign," the King of the Netherworld said, "you have indeed passed through them. That your hair has gradually turned yellow was the first sign.
That your teeth have gradually become loose was the second sign. That your strength has gradually declined was the third sign.
That your ears and eyes have gradually grown dim and deaf was the fourth and fifth signs. The signs have passed through you many times. There is a youth here who weeps."
He replied, "I have attained faith, yet I am not yet fully enlightened. The King of the Netherworld said, "Your attainments are already many.
Do you still remember that certain youth who died of illness and perished from an epidemic? That certain youth who died by a knife wound or by hanging?
That certain youth who drowned, was burned by fire, devoured by a wolf, or stung by a snake? All these were instances of your faith. How could this be otherwise?"

One must certainly call out one's name and announce it. Even if you possess the world-shaking courage of Mount Ren and the talent that overturns heaven and earth, can you truly escape the interrogations of this place?

Only by remaining transcendentally aloof from worldly affairs can one not only avoid these interrogations, but even cause the King of the Netherworld to revere and pay homage; and that means nothing other than reciting the Buddha’s name.
As for those who attain rebirth, they are like moths that fly into a lamp.
That these moths die in the oil and flame is not because they die from the oil and flame; rather, they die from the act of seeing. So it is with humans.
If one pities them and drives them away, they will surely seize the opportunity to throw themselves [into the fire]. They think to themselves:
"What I have seen must not be mistaken; therefore, I shall press forward without turning back until death. This is because people crave sound and beauty, and they crave wealth and profit.

As for those who are addicted to gambling, because their vision is limited to this alone, they press forward with single-minded determination until death ends it all. Why not take the moth as a lesson?

Regarding the fly’s delusion within the window: when a fly is at a window, it circles and hovers back and forth, unable to exit for the entire day because it is constrained by what it perceives and cannot take even a single step back.
If it could suddenly and decisively take that one step back, everywhere would be open.
The ocean is vast and the sky is wide. This Sahā world is but a single large window-frame.

From antiquity until now, one knows not how many foolish flies have been shut within it. I am fortunate that I have suddenly taken a step back and am flying toward the West. I fly toward the West! How joyful!
Regarding the four methods for training horses:
In the world of the Buddha, there were those who trained excellent steeds. The Buddha asked what methods they employed, and they replied that they used four:

first, kindness; second, severity; third, severity first followed by kindness; and fourth, kindness first followed by severity. The Buddha said, "These four methods do not truly train [the mind]. He then led [the discussion further].
"What should be done? The Master of Horses replied, "One should simply kill them. "When the World-Honored One teaches and transforms sentient beings, what methods should he employ?
The Buddha said, "He likewise employs four methods. The first is employing kindness, which refers to those who possess good faith;

one instructs them in the practice and study of the Way. The second is employing awe, which refers to those who commit evil; one shows them the revolving cycle of the three miserable realms. The third is..."
"First, he taught them to practice and study the Way. Fourthly, he first showed them the cycle of rebirth within the three miserable realms.
Master Ma asked, "If these four methods do not transform them, what shall we do? The Buddha said, "I shall also kill them. Master Ma said, "The Tathāgata possesses great compassion."
"Why did he carry out the killing? The Buddha said, "There are four types of people who cannot be transformed; even instruction is of no benefit. He then refused to speak with him.
Because he would not speak with him, [the man] killed him.

Regarding the Eye Medicine: When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, Queen Māyā (the consort of King Śuddhodana), while in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, experienced several types of evil dreams.
Among them was one dream wherein she saw the sun disk of the lower realm suddenly set, leaving the entire world in darkness.
There were countless rākṣasas holding sharp knives in their hands, gouging out the eyes of the people of the world.
Māyā sighed and said, "This must surely be an omen that my son, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, will enter nirvāṇa. Shortly thereafter, the Venerable Aniruddha—
Indeed, he has ascended to heaven to report this. Those books in the world that slander the Triple Gem are all those which gouge out the eyes of people.
As the merit-power of people in the final age becomes increasingly shallow, such books become more numerous;
as their wisdom becomes increasingly feeble, those who revere such books become more numerous. Therefore, those with merit must act early.
To awaken for oneself and not be pierced by it is truly the highest state. Should one nevertheless be wounded by it, one should quickly apply an excellent medicine.
Where is this medicine? This book is one such remedy.
There is a vow that will surely be fulfilled:
Lu Wenzheng Gong Mengzheng of the Song dynasty, whose courtesy name was Shengong, was the first to pass the jinshi examination during the reign of Emperor Taizong and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Xu.

Every morning when he rose to perform his prostrations before the Buddha, he would invariably offer this prayer: "May those who do not believe in the Buddha never be born into my family. May it be so.
My descendants have, for generations, partaken of the imperial bounty and protected the Triple Gem. Later, my son Yijian was enfeoffed as the Duke of Shen;
every New Year’s Day, after performing his prostrations at the family shrine, he would immediately pay his respects to Chan Master Guanghui.
Yijian’s son, Gongzhu, was likewise enfeoffed as the Duke of Shen, and he treated Chan Master Tianyi in the same manner. Hao Wen, the Vice President of the Left, [treated] Yuan...
Chan Master Foguo Zhaoying was also like this. Yongzhong, the son of the Vice President [Wen Zheng], was likewise toward Chan Master Foguo Zhaoying.

For generations, they have been illustrious and noble while serving the Buddha, truly fulfilling the official’s wish. Now, what Wen Zheng expected was merely a worldly aspiration, yet he was still able to achieve it;
how much more so for one who has resolved to attain Bodhicitta and vows to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*)—how could such a person not succeed in their quest?
One who is a monk must not fail to cultivate the Pure Land.
The Chan Master Qingcaotang of the Song dynasty was always possessed of pure preceptual conduct. When he was over ninety years old, the Zeng family regularly provided him with offerings.
He repeatedly bestowed clothing and other necessities upon the monks, who were moved by his virtue and granted him permission to be reborn into his family.
Later, when the wife of the Zeng clan gave birth to a son, she sent someone to check on the hermitage; the master had already passed away while sitting in meditation.

The son born was none other than Zeng Gong (Zeng Xi), who, because he had cultivated merit and wisdom in a previous life, attained high honors in the civil service at a young age and later served as a worthy prime minister. This is similar to what occurred during the late Ming dynasty...
The monk Dacheng of Zhejiang was collecting leftover rice from alms bowls to provide for the assembly at his monastery.
On his way, he passed by the home of the Shi family, who were devoted Buddhists; whenever a monk came to beg for food, they would invariably invite him to stay.

When Dacheng returned to the temple with the collected rice, the Shi family noticed that his portion was small each day and would always supplement it until it was full. The Shi family had long been childless, but subsequently, their wife suddenly became pregnant. They divided [the merit].
At the time of delivery, Chengda personally saw Da-cheng enter the bedroom. He hurriedly pursued him, but could not find him; yet the woman giving birth eventually delivered a son.
On that day, Da-cheng did not appear to collect his rice. When Chengda went to the temple to inquire about him, he learned that Da-cheng had passed away on that very day.
Thereupon, the child was named after him. In his youth, the boy was exceptionally intelligent.
Xiaoyou observed the *ruci* (vegetarian) fast during his pregnancy and maintained his precepts without violation throughout his life.
In the year Yiwu of the Shunzhi era, he became the grand champion of the empire. From a secular perspective, these two gentlemen were both wealthy, noble, and enjoyed great fame.
However, from the perspective of those who cultivate the Way, both monks made many errors. Had the two masters known the Dharma-gate of the Western Land [Buddhism], they would have...
As for those who practice, they dedicate their merit toward the Pure Land. Even if one cannot attain the highest grade, one may still achieve the middle grade;
why must one limit the scope of their endeavor solely to becoming a top scholar or a prime minister?
High monks should also cultivate the Pure Land.

Shi Xuanjing of Xiangzhou during the Sui dynasty was proficient in both the doctrinal and practical aspects of the teachings, and his reputation for the Way spread far and wide. In the sixth month of the second year of the Daye era, he...
As he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he bathed and sat upright with his two eyes gazing upward.
Suddenly, he spoke of his own accord: "I wish to be born in the Tuṣita Inner Court to see Maitreya Bodhisattva; why then would I become the King of the Yāma Heaven?

When the assembly questioned him, he replied, "This is not something you can know. A short while later, he said again, "It is very busy in the heavens, and there are many guests. Thereupon, he sat [and passed away].
Alas! When you, Master, were practicing the Way, you originally resolved to see Maitreya; yet here, unable to see Maitreya, you have instead become a heavenly king.
From a worldly perspective, your rank is already above that of the High God (Shangdi).
Nevertheless, compared to being born in the Western Land [of Sukhāvatī], this falls far short. Thus we know that even eminent monks cannot [attain the ultimate goal].
If one does not cultivate the Pure Land,
one cannot bear to willingly become a ghost within the great trichiliocosm.
Among all human beings— whether noble or base, wise or foolish, old or young, male or female— at the moment of death, [this applies to all].

Afterwards, if one does not appear in the world, there is no one who will not become a ghost. To exhort people to recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Pure Land is to exhort the people of the world not to go and become ghosts.
Yet the petty Confucians do not believe in the Buddha-dharma and instead follow along in slandering it.
Not only do they willingly become ghosts themselves, but they also wish to urge all people of the world to become ghosts as well.
Those who are not ghosts at present are merely so for the time being. All these countless people before our eyes will, in the blink of an eye, become that same multitude of ghosts.
People simply do not realize how extremely transient this is; therefore, they exhaust their bodies and weary themselves.

People seek wealth and status through divine means, yet they never obtain them; even if they should attain extreme wealth and status, at the moment of their departure, they cannot carry a single coin in their hands.
A ghost merely calls out and they must depart immediately—what, then, is the point of such wealth and status?
Only those who practice the Buddha-recitation reach this state without illness or calamity, passing away peacefully and with ease. Their bodies...
One shall be free from all illness, suffering, and calamity; the mind shall be devoid of all attachment and delusion. When malevolent spirits behold one’s shadow, they will vanish;
when King Yama hears one’s name, he will prostrate himself in reverence. Is this not the mark of a great man who has transcended the world?
Only when a person attains such a state can they truly avoid becoming a ghost. Thus, it is indeed not easy to avoid becoming a ghost.
The nine classes of beings shall all attain rebirth there.
These nine classes are: namely, those born from the womb, those born from eggs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation; those with form and those without form;

those with perception, those without perception, and those with neither perception nor non-perception. These nine classes encompass the entirety of the noble and the lowly, the hidden and the manifest, as well as the heavens above.
Such is the nature of the world. Among the nine categories of existence, the most suffering are the three evil realms;
the most joyful are the twenty-eight heavens within the triple world. Yet, because one has not yet transcended birth and death, one cycles through the six paths of rebirth.
Thus, while those in suffering are certainly miserable, those in joy are likewise subject to suffering. Even for the long-lived devas who currently enjoy boundless pleasure, nevertheless—

When the heavenly rewards of merit are exhausted, one still falls into the three miserable realms; how can this compare to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where one is forever liberated from saṃsāra and eternally parts with the six destinies?
I have often offered incense and performed prostrations in the temples of Wenchang, Lord Guan, and the Eastern Peak, after which I invariably made this vow:
"I pray that the Honored Lord may place faith in the Triple Gem, resolve upon the Bodhicitta, and attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land. Thus I act.
The Bodhisattva Path. Furthermore, I have once prostrated before the Honored Celestial Mother and the Supreme Lord of Heaven (Hao Tian Shang Di).

Although I was filled with utmost sincerity and trepidation, following my kowtows and prostrations, I also prayed that these Most Honorable Ones would practice mindfulness of the Buddha to attain rebirth in the Pure Land and cultivate the Bodhisattva path to universally deliver all beings.
Why is this? It is simply because those who possess wisdom perceive the most sublime and lofty matters within the world.
Nothing is like the recitation of the Buddha's name; there is no practice more meritorious than rebirth in the Pure Land.

Rebirth through the recitation of the Buddha’s name cannot be compared with any other form of merit. The Honored Deity Doushu (Yoginī) is none other than the Bodhisattva Mārīcī mentioned in the sutras.
The Great Heaven Supreme God is the very Trāyastriṃśa Heavenly King mentioned in the sutras.

Whenever the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma, there is no Trāyastriṃśa Heavenly King who does not respectfully prostrate and stand in attendance at his side. Hearing this silent prayer today, he will surely rejoice;
there is absolutely no possibility that he would instead bring about offenses or calamities. It is our great fortune to have encountered this Dharma gate. Not...
One who possesses courageous and vigorous diligence and dedicates it toward Bodhi— is this not indeed what the Tathāgata calls most worthy of compassion?
Thus, one should contemplate the Buddha’s power of non-wasteful application.
In worldly affairs, if a plan fails to succeed, all prior effort is utterly wasted.

Only in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is it the case that even if one begins but does not finish, what has been recited in the past will never have been in vain. Long ago, there was a woodcutter who encountered a tiger while climbing a tree.

If merely reciting "Namo Buddha" once leads one to rely upon it for renunciation and gradually attain Buddhahood after many births and kalpas, how much more so for those who practice with sincerity throughout their entire lives?
Even if one cannot achieve rebirth in the Pure Land in this present life, one will certainly transcend birth and death in a future existence.
This is not like the worldly pursuit of study that fails to reach its goal, wasting one's spirit, or an enterprise that fails despite its management, resulting instead in regret.
This means to squander one's capital.
Among the superior matters of the human world, none compare to the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation).
The *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Parables) states: "In the past, there was a husband and wife who prayed to Heaven for a child. The wife soon became pregnant and gave birth to four [sons]."
There were four kinds of objects: first, a *kudava* measure of sandalwood rice; second, a jar of nectar-like honey; third, a precious jewel-embroidered pouch;
and fourth, a seven-jointed divine staff. The man sighed and said, "I originally sought a son; what use have I for these objects? The deity asked, "Why do you wish to obtain a son?
The man replied, "I wish to obtain a son, hoping that he will provide me with support and care. The deity—
He said, "The rice within the measure-dipper becomes full again as soon as it is taken; the jar of nectar can eliminate a hundred ailments; the pouch of precious jewels is inexhaustible when used;
and the divine staff of seven joints is prepared to ward off violence. How could a filial son among men achieve such things?
The man was greatly delighted and subsequently attained great wealth. Later, other countries heard of this and dispatched troops to seize it. His...
When a person holds up a staff, [the deity] flies through the air to strike back and drive them away, protecting them for their entire life.

Among worldly people who strive and toil incessantly, finding no leisure for spiritual practice, it is generally only for the sake of a wife and children. Yet, even if a wife and children were to serve one with the utmost devotion, how could they ever be like these four objects?
As for attaining rebirth in the Western Paradise, one transcends birth and death, adorned with myriad blessings; this is what is truly sought.

It is as you wish. Furthermore, how could it possibly be measured by these four things? Therefore, among all the most supreme matters in the heavens and among humans, none surpasses the recitation of the Buddha's name.
